::: {.callout-note title="Chapter overview"}
One set of records can owe several answers. Using the 98 occupations of
Chapter 7 that have a recorded type, this chapter asks how income varies
with education, how it differs with education at the same prestige,
percentage of women and type, and whether a fuller learning rule predicts
held-out occupations better than education alone. We see what a partial
slope compares and why it can differ from the marginal slope, estimate
and check it, calculate a fitted profile and a standardized average,
answer the prediction question with shared held-out folds, and then read
and evaluate the three reported answers and their synthesis. By the end
you will be able to fit and read an additive multiple regression in R,
keep changes of records, comparison, coefficient coordinates and
uncertainty calculation apart, judge a held-out comparison, and evaluate
coordinated answers without merging them.
:::

A report on occupational income may ask whether education and income move
together, whether that relationship remains when other characteristics of
the occupations are held constant, and whether those characteristics help
predict income. The questions inform one another, but answering one does
not answer the other two.

We use a **retrospective teaching study written for this chapter**. Its
records are the *Prestige* data distributed with the carData package
[@carData2022; @fox2019], whose documentation describes the data; the
analyses and the short report are ours.

Chapter 5's partial correlation held one variable fixed by residualizing,
removing that variable's fitted linear part from two others before
correlating what remained. A fitted equation with several predictors
holds the others fixed directly, because two of its fitted means that
differ in one predictor share every other term. This chapter applies that
idea to several controls at once, tracks the full model's uncertainty,
and separates a comparison at fixed values from an average over named
profiles. Chapter 9, Section 2, applies the same idea to adjusted group
means in the analysis of covariance.

\clearpage

## Three Questions in One Set of Records {#sec-ch8-questions}

### Three questions, three answers

```{=latex}
\Needspace{20\baselineskip}
```

| Pair and role | Question | Estimand and owed answer |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **1. Contextual description** | How does income vary linearly with education across the 98 retained occupations? | The finite-record marginal least-squares slope; a descriptive answer for these records |
| **2. Primary conditional association** | How does income differ with education at the same prestige, percentage of women, and type, within support? | The linear conditional-mean coefficient $\beta_E$ under the declared working model; fitted $b_E$ is its estimate from the 98 retained records |
| **3. Secondary prediction analysis** | Does the full additive learning rule predict eligible same-source occupation records with lower expected absolute error than the education-only rule? | Difference in expected absolute error of the two learning procedures at the declared training sizes; an internal validation answer |

: Three separately owed answers in the occupation teaching study. {#tbl-ch8-pairs tbl-colwidths="[22,36,42]"}

Each row is a question--answer pair with **one argument with linked
layers**. The three are not statistical strands of one argument: the
report owes separate conclusions about marginal association, conditional
association, and prediction. Estimands become strands only when one
integrated conclusion needs them all, and printing several coefficients
creates neither extra questions nor extra strands.

### The occupation records

A row is an **occupation**, not a worker. Income is the occupation's
average annual income in 1971 Canadian dollars, divided here by 1,000;
education is average years of education; *women* is the percentage of
women; prestige is a rating from a mid-1960s survey, earlier than the
1971 income and education; and type is blue-collar (*bc*),
professional/managerial/technical (*prof*), or white-collar (*wc*). These
historical occupational averages are not current individual earnings.

Chapter 7 used all 102 occupations. The full variable set leaves 98
complete records, because athletes, newsboys, babysitters, and farmers
have no recorded type; the three types keep 44, 31, and 23 records. We
keep the source row order, which also makes the validation split of
Section 6 reproducible, and the chapter's code runs in order from here in
a fresh R session.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{20\baselineskip}
```

```{r}
#| label: ch8-records
#| echo: true
all_occ <- carData::Prestige
all_occ$occupation <- rownames(all_occ)
all_occ$income_k <- all_occ$income / 1000
all_occ$type <- factor(all_occ$type, levels = c("bc", "prof", "wc"))
vars <- c("income_k", "education", "prestige", "women", "type")
d <- all_occ[complete.cases(all_occ[, vars]), ]
c(original = nrow(all_occ), retained = nrow(d))
table(d$type)
```

We refit the education-only model on these **same 98 records** before any
adjusted comparison, so that the move from 102 to 98, a change in which
records are described, is never presented as an adjustment effect.
Complete records make the computations comparable; they do not make the
omitted occupations irrelevant or the 98 a probability sample of Canadian
occupations.

### What each answer estimates

Pair 1 describes these records: once the records and the least-squares
rule are fixed, its slope is simply calculated.

Pair 2 targets $\beta_E$, the education coefficient in a declared working
model whose mean income is linear in education, prestige, women, and
type; the fitted $b_E$ estimates it from the 98 records. Like Pair 1's
slope, $b_E$ is exactly calculable, but it is an estimate of $\beta_E$,
not a second finite-record target. An interval for $\beta_E$ adds
assumptions: occupation incomes vary independently around that linear
mean, with a common error variance for the classical interval and Normal
errors for its exact $t$ reference. The HC3 interval of Section 3.3
relaxes the common variance under its own large-sample conditions.
Neither interval creates independence or linearity, and neither claims
verified probability sampling or randomized education. Section 4 checks
how far the working model can be trusted.

A **best linear projection**, which summarizes a curved relationship over
a stated distribution of predictors, is a different declared target, not
a rescue adopted after curvature appears; Chapter 9, Appendix A,
develops it.

Pair 3 imagines a different repetition: train a rule on eligible,
exchangeable same-source records, then predict a record whose outcome
was not used in training. Pair 2's coefficient interval cannot justify
that answer.

## Marginal and Conditional Comparisons {#sec-ch8-comparisons}

### What a partial slope compares

Chapter 5's partial correlation held a variable fixed by residualizing
both variables on it. A fitted equation holds its other predictors fixed
directly: change one predictor, keep the others at the same values, and
subtract the two fitted means.

Let $e$ be education, $p$ prestige, $w$ percentage of women, and $t$ type.
The fitted additive equation is

$$
\widehat m(e,p,w,t)
 =b_0+b_Ee+b_Pp+b_Ww
   +b_{\mathrm{prof}}D_{\mathrm{prof}}
   +b_{\mathrm{wc}}D_{\mathrm{wc}},
$$

where an indicator $D$ is 1 for its named type and 0 otherwise, so
blue-collar, with both indicators zero, is the reference type. The model
has six coefficients, including its intercept. For two profiles with the
same $p,w,t$ whose education differs by one year,

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\widehat m(e+1,p,w,t)-\widehat m(e,p,w,t)\\
&\qquad=b_E(e+1)-b_Ee=b_E.
\end{aligned}
$$

All the shared terms cancel, so $b_E$ compares modeled occupation-level
income at the **same prestige, percentage of women, and type**, and a
two-year difference corresponds to $2b_E$.

"Holding constant" names this comparison of fitted means. It does not
mean that education was changed experimentally, that two observed
occupations match on everything else, or that unmeasured differences are
controlled. The additive form also assumes the same education comparison
at every value of the other predictors; letting that comparison vary is
the interaction question of Chapter 10.

### Why the marginal slope can differ

A known process makes the difference visible. Suppose

$$
Y=50+2X+5Z+\varepsilon,
\qquad E(\varepsilon\mid X,Z)=0,
$$

with finite variances and
$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)/\operatorname{Var}(X)=0.65$.
The conditional $X$ coefficient is 2, and the marginal linear slope is

$$
\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}
=2+5\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}
=2+5(0.65)=5.25.
$$

@fig-ch8-known-process draws one generated sample of 250 cases from this
process, with the process's own mean lines rather than fitted ones. Each
solid line holds $Z$ at one value and rises 2 for each unit of $X$. The
dashed marginal line rises 5.25, because higher $X$ comes with higher $Z$
(the darker points sit toward the upper right) and the marginal line
carries that association along.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ch8-known-process
#| fig-cap: "One generated sample from the known process, with its marginal line and three lines at fixed $Z$."
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of 250 generated points of Y against standardized X, shaded by Z, with darker points higher and to the right. Three parallel solid lines at Z equal to minus one, zero and one rise with slope 2. A steeper dashed line, the marginal line, rises with slope 5.25 and crosses the three solid lines."
#| fig-width: 6.1
#| fig-height: 3.5
RNGkind("Mersenne-Twister", "Inversion", "Rejection")
set.seed(82108)
ch8a_n <- 250
ch8a_x <- rnorm(ch8a_n)
ch8a_z <- .65 * ch8a_x + sqrt(1 - .65^2) * rnorm(ch8a_n)
ch8a_y <- 50 + 2 * ch8a_x + 5 * ch8a_z + rnorm(ch8a_n, sd = 6)
ch8a_sim <- data.frame(strategy = ch8a_x, prior = ch8a_z,
                       score = ch8a_y)
ch8_lines <- data.frame(prior = c(-1, 0, 1),
                        intercept = 50 + 5 * c(-1, 0, 1))
ggplot2::ggplot(ch8a_sim, ggplot2::aes(strategy, score)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(colour = prior), size = 1.2,
                      alpha = .8) +
  ggplot2::geom_abline(data = ch8_lines,
                       ggplot2::aes(intercept = intercept, slope = 2),
                       colour = "#245C78", linewidth = .8) +
  ggplot2::geom_abline(intercept = 50, slope = 5.25, linetype = 2,
                       linewidth = .9) +
  ggplot2::annotate("text", x = 3.1, y = 50 + 2 * 3.1 + 5 * c(-1, 0, 1),
                    label = c("Z = -1", "Z = 0", "Z = 1"),
                    hjust = 0, vjust = -0.35, size = 3.1,
                    colour = "#245C78") +
  ggplot2::annotate("text", x = -2.6, y = 74, hjust = 0, vjust = 1,
                    size = 3.1,
                    label = "Dashed: marginal line, slope 5.25\nSolid: fixed Z, slope 2") +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_gradient(low = "grey85", high = "black") +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-2.6, 3.6), breaks = -2:3) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "X (standardized)", y = "Y", colour = "Z")
```

The two slopes answer different questions: one holds $Z$ fixed, the
other includes how $Z$ moves with $X$, and neither alone says what would
happen if someone intervened on $X$. Calling 5.25 "biased" requires
naming the target it is used for; as the marginal linear slope it is
correct. Appendix A gives the derivation and the repeated samples.

Not every change to a model changes the scientific estimand. In a
randomized study, well-specified covariate adjustment can estimate the
same declared average assignment effect more precisely; releveling a
factor changes the coefficient coordinates but not the fitted values;
and a different uncertainty estimator changes the interval but not the
coefficient.

\Needspace{9\baselineskip}

### Indicators and a fitted profile

The full occupation fit, displayed to four decimal places, is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\mathrm{income}}_k
={}&0.4205+0.1164e+0.1406p-0.0535w\\
 &+0.3242D_{\mathrm{prof}}+0.2353D_{\mathrm{wc}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For a white-collar profile with education 11, prestige 45, and women 50,
$D_{\mathrm{prof}}=0$ and $D_{\mathrm{wc}}=1$, and the unrounded fitted
coefficients give

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat m_*
={}&\widehat\beta_0+11\widehat\beta_E+45\widehat\beta_P
+50\widehat\beta_W+\widehat\delta_{\mathrm{wc}}\\
\approx{}&5.5886,
\end{aligned}
$$

a fitted mean of about 5,589 dollars on the historical income scale, not
a guarantee for any occupation or worker.

Do these three values occur together among the white-collar records?
Separate ranges cannot say. A **convex combination** of records is a
weighted average whose weights are nonnegative and sum to one, and a
**joint-support witness** is a convex combination of observed records
that returns the profile. The four white-collar records in
@tbl-ch8-profile-support, weighted as listed, return education 11,
prestige 45, and women 50 at once.

\Needspace{11\baselineskip}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ch8-profile-support
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Four observed white-collar records recover the declared profile."
support_names <- c("radio.tv.announcers", "tellers.cashiers",
                   "receptionsts", "sales.supervisors")
support_rows <- d[support_names, c("education", "prestige", "women")]
support_weights <- c(0.245243736035, 0.230972611567,
                     0.226143656937, 0.297639995461)
support_display <- data.frame(
  Occupation = c("Radio/TV announcers", "Tellers/cashiers",
                 "Receptionists", "Sales supervisors"),
  support_rows,
  Weight = sub("^0", "", format(round(unname(support_weights), 4),
    digits = 15, scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)),
  row.names = NULL
)
knitr::kable(support_display,
  col.names = c("Occupation", "Education", "Prestige", "Women", "Weight"),
  digits = c(0, 2, 1, 2, 4), align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

The four weights are positive and sum to one; the table rounds them, and
the Computer Lab checks the averages at full precision. The witness places the profile
inside the joint covariate hull of the white-collar records on all three
continuous predictors. It does not show that many occupations lie near
the profile, that one matches it exactly, or that a causal comparison is
supported.

The intercept refers to zero education, prestige, and women in the
reference type; it anchors the fitted surface and need not describe a
plausible occupation. Nor is one type coefficient "the effect of
occupational type". In Chapter 6's indicator fit the factor stood alone,
so each coefficient was a difference between group means; here each type
coefficient compares fitted means at the same education, prestige, and
women. Appendix A gives the group-mean and releveling calculations, and
Chapter 9 develops contrasts, block tests, and the analysis-of-variance
identity.

## Estimating the Partial Slope {#sec-ch8-estimate}

### Three models on the same rows

Least squares fits a multiple regression as it fitted Chapter 7's line,
choosing the coefficients that make the residual sum of squares
smallest. We fit three models to the same 98 rows.

```{r}
#| label: ch8-fits
#| echo: true
m0 <- lm(income_k ~ education, data = d)
m1 <- lm(income_k ~ education + prestige, data = d)
m2 <- lm(income_k ~ education + prestige + women + type, data = d)
coef(m2)
```

| Records and specification | Education slope | In-sample $R^2$ | Role here |
|:--|--:|--:|:--|
| Earlier 102, education only | 0.8988 | .3336 | Earlier result; not the adjustment baseline |
| Same 98, education only | 0.8830 | .3296 | Pair 1's marginal description |
| Same 98, education and prestige | $-0.2179$ | .4996 | Intermediate comparison |
| Same 98, full declared predictors | 0.1164 | .6362 | Pair 2's estimate of $\beta_E$ |

: The model sequence separates sample composition from adjustment. {#tbl-ch8-sequence tbl-colwidths="[36,18,16,30]"}

*Note.* Slopes are thousand 1971 Canadian dollars per education year.
These are fitted summaries, not causal effects. No sampling interval is
attached to Pair 1's finite-record estimand.

Education and prestige are highly correlated here, $r=.8665$. Once
prestige enters, the education comparison uses only the education
variation that prestige does not linearly account for, and women and
type change the conditioning set again. The movement from 0.8830 to
$-0.2179$ to 0.1164 is a sequence of named comparisons in a small
observational record, not a true effect being "explained away".

When predictors are added and both fits use the same rows, the residual
sum of squares cannot increase, so $R^2$ cannot fall; its rise describes
training fit, not held-out prediction (Section 6).

### The partial slope from residuals {#ch08-partial-regression}

Multiple regression still uses Chapter 7's covariance-to-slope
reasoning, now after removing several controls. Regress education on
prestige, percentage of women, and type and keep the residuals
$r_{E,i}$; do the same for income to obtain $r_{Y,i}$. Both auxiliary
fits include an intercept and use exactly the 98 rows of the full fit.
Then

$$
b_E=\frac{\sum_i r_{E,i}r_{Y,i}}{\sum_i r_{E,i}^2}
    =r_{EY\cdot Z}\frac{s_{r_Y}}{s_{r_E}},
$$

where $Z$ denotes the control columns and $r_{EY\cdot Z}$, the
correlation of the two residual vectors, is the partial correlation. The
numerator is the linear co-variation left after the controls and the
denominator the education variation left; the ratio of residual SDs turns
the unit-free correlation into thousand dollars per education year.

The uncertainty must count the fitted controls. Prestige and women supply
one column each and type two, so with education and the intercept the
model estimates $p=6$ coefficients from $n=98$ rows, leaving $n-p=92$
residual degrees of freedom. With the full model's residual sum of
squares, $RSS_{\mathrm{full}}$,

$$
SE(b_E)=\sqrt{\frac{RSS_{\mathrm{full}}/(n-p)}
                         {\sum_i r_{E,i}^2}},
\qquad
t_E=r_{EY\cdot Z}\sqrt{\frac{n-p}{1-r_{EY\cdot Z}^2}}.
$$

The slope identity is algebraic; the SE and the $t_{92}$ reference for
$H_0:\beta_E=0$ rest on the classical model of Section 1.3. In
@tbl-ch8-partial-df the first row is the full model's education row,
which these formulas reproduce, and the second is a fresh fit of residual
income on residual education.

\Needspace{10\baselineskip}

| Calculation on the same 98 rows | Slope | SE | df | $t$ | $p$ |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Full model `m2`, education row; the residual formulas with $n-p=92$ | 0.1164 | 0.2752 | 92 | 0.4230 | .6732 |
| A fresh fit of residual income on residual education | 0.1164 | 0.2694 | 96 | 0.4321 | .6666 |

: The residual slope reproduces the full-model coefficient; only the full model's df gives its uncertainty. {#tbl-ch8-partial-df tbl-colwidths="[44,11,11,8,12,14]"}

Both rows share the slope 0.1164 and the partial correlation .0441. The
fresh fit counts $98-2=96$ df, as if fitting the four control columns had
cost nothing, so its SE is smaller by the factor $\sqrt{92/96}$. Use
`m2`, or the formulas with $n-p=92$, for uncertainty.

Covariance now has two meanings. Chapter 5's `cov()` describes how
recorded variables spread and move together; `vcov()` estimates the
covariance of the fitted coefficients. @tbl-ch8-covariance-objects
compares them on the same 98 rows.

\Needspace{16\baselineskip}

| | Recorded-data covariance | Coefficient covariance |
|:--|:--|:--|
| R call | `cov()` of income, education, prestige and women | `vcov(m2)` |
| Rows and columns | 4 numeric variables; the type factor is left out | 6 fitted coefficients, including the intercept and two type indicators |
| Diagonal entries | Sample variances | Squared coefficient SEs |
| Off-diagonal entries | Sample covariances between variables | Joint uncertainty of two coefficients |
| Education entry | 7.5567 years squared | 0.0757; its square root is the SE 0.2752 |
| Question it answers | How the recorded variables spread and move together across occupations | How uncertain the fitted coefficients are, and how their errors move together |

: Two covariance matrices from the same 98 records answer different questions. {#tbl-ch8-covariance-objects tbl-colwidths="[22,39,39]"}

The education entries differ by a factor of about 100 because they
measure different things: the spread of education across occupations
and the squared uncertainty of one fitted coefficient. The matrices are
not interchangeable; Section 5 uses the coefficient covariance in
$\mathbf x_*^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\mathbf V}\mathbf x_*$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ch8-partial
#| fig-cap: "Marginal and residualized income--education comparisons in the same 98 occupations."
#| fig-alt: "The marginal scatterplot has a positive fitted line. After linearly removing prestige, women, and type from both variables, the fitted line is nearly flat and substantial residual variation remains."
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 3.5
r_E <- residuals(lm(education ~ prestige + women + type, data = d))
r_Y <- residuals(lm(income_k ~ prestige + women + type, data = d))
oldpar <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.3, 4.2, 1, .5), mgp = c(2.7, .8, 0))
plot(d$education, d$income_k, pch = 1, xlab = "Education (years)",
     ylab = "Income (thousand dollars)")
abline(m0, col = "#245C78", lwd = 2)
plot(r_E, r_Y, pch = 1, xlab = "Residual education (years)",
     ylab = "Residual income (thousand dollars)")
abline(a = 0, b = coef(m2)["education"], col = "#245C78", lwd = 2)
par(oldpar)
```

@fig-ch8-partial sets the two comparisons side by side. The marginal
line rises 0.8830 per year; after the fitted linear parts of prestige,
women, and type are removed from both variables, the residual line rises
only 0.1164, with wide scatter around it. Residualizing removes those
**fitted linear components**, not every substantive difference between
occupations. Chapter 9 develops the matrix version.

### Interval and test for the partial slope

With 92 residual degrees of freedom, the classical 95% interval for
education is

$$
\begin{aligned}
b_E\pm t_{.975,92}SE(b_E)
 &=0.1164\pm1.9861(0.2752)\\
 &\approx[-0.4302,\ 0.6631].
\end{aligned}
$$

Under the classical assumptions the interval is compatible with negative
and positive conditional slopes, including differences of several
hundred dollars per year of education. With no margin of practical
equivalence declared, the direction and the practically relevant size
remain unresolved; the interval does not show that the slope is zero or
that adjustment has removed an effect of education.

```{r}
#| label: ch8-uncertainty
#| echo: true
confint(m2, "education")
hc3_covariance <- sandwich::vcovHC(m2, type = "HC3")
hc3_se <- sqrt(hc3_covariance["education", "education"])
coef(m2)["education"] + c(-1, 1) * qt(.975, 92) * hc3_se
```

HC3 keeps the coefficient and replaces its covariance estimate, giving
SE 0.3823 and, with the same $t_{92}$ convention, the approximate
interval $[-0.6429,0.8758]$. It allows unequal error variances among
independent observations under large-sample conditions and is not an
exact small-sample guarantee. Neither interval allows for unmodeled
dependence, selection, measurement error, or a wrong mean form.

The matching test addresses $H_0:\beta_E=0$ in the stated full model,
not "education has no effect". Its classical $t=0.423$ and $p=.6732$ do
not prove the null, and the test does not decide which of the three
questions deserves an answer.

\Needspace{12\baselineskip}

## Checking the Model {#sec-ch8-check}

Checking asks what the model leaves unexplained and what follows for the
answer; no single graph passes or fails the model.

### Residuals, leverage, and influence

A residual is an observed deviation from a fitted value, not the
unobserved error. Leverage measures how unusual a record's combination
of predictor values is; a high-leverage record pulls the fit toward
itself, so its residual tends to be smaller. A standardized residual
therefore divides each residual by its own estimated SD, which combines
the common residual scale with the record's leverage, and an externally
studentized residual does the same with the scale estimated with that
record left out. Influence, measured by Cook's distance, combines
leverage with the size of the residual [@cook1977]. The extraction lists
the five occupations with the largest Cook's distance.

\Needspace{18\baselineskip}

```{r}
#| label: ch8-diagnostics
#| echo: true
ch8_diag <- data.frame(
  occupation = rownames(d), fitted = fitted(m2),
  residual = residuals(m2), standardized = rstandard(m2),
  studentized = rstudent(m2), leverage = hatvalues(m2),
  cooks = cooks.distance(m2)
)
ch8_top <- order(ch8_diag$cooks, decreasing = TRUE)[1:5]
ch8_diag[ch8_top, c("residual", "studentized", "leverage", "cooks")]
```

@fig-ch8-diagnostics shows four views. If the linear mean described the
records well, the residuals in panel (a) would scatter evenly around zero
with a flat smooth; here the smooth drifts downward and the scatter
widens at high fitted income. With constant spread, the smooth in panel
(b) would stay level; it rises. Panel (c) follows the Normal reference
line in the middle but departs in both tails, most strongly on the
right, where a few occupations earn far more than the model predicts;
on the left, ministers earn far less. The two largest positive
residuals, general managers and physicians in the printed list, also
have the largest Cook's distances, drawn as the biggest circles in
panel (d).

```{r}
#| label: fig-ch8-diagnostics
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Four complementary diagnostic views for the full additive model."
#| fig-alt: >
#|   Residual and scale plots show structure and changing spread.
#|   A normal quantile plot departs in both tails, most strongly on
#|   the right. The final panel relates leverage and studentized
#|   residuals, with point sizes indicating Cook's distance.
#| fig-width: 6.7
#| fig-height: 6.2
local({
  old <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
  on.exit(par(old))
  par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
  z <- ch8_diag
  plot(z$fitted, z$residual, pch = 1,
       xlab = "Fitted income", ylab = "Residual",
       main = "(a) Mean pattern")
  abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
  lines(lowess(z$fitted, z$residual), lwd = 2)
  plot(z$fitted, sqrt(abs(z$standardized)), pch = 1,
       xlab = "Fitted income", ylab = "Sqrt |standardized|",
       main = "(b) Scale pattern")
  lines(lowess(z$fitted, sqrt(abs(z$standardized))), lwd = 2)
  qqnorm(z$studentized, pch = 1, main = "(c) Normal reference")
  qqline(z$studentized, lwd = 2)
  plot(z$leverage, z$studentized, pch = 1,
       cex = .8 + 2 * sqrt(z$cooks / max(z$cooks)),
       xlab = "Leverage", ylab = "Studentized residual",
       main = "(d) Influence")
  abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
})
```

These features challenge the linear mean form and the constant-variance
description, and the heavy tails matter for exact small-sample
Normal-theory inference, although OLS can still be calculated. A large
residual, high leverage, and high influence are different features, and
none alone shows that a record is invalid. No residual graph can
establish that occupations are independent draws from a wider
population.

### Joint support and collinearity

Joint support concerns combinations of predictor values. Section 2.3's
witness established it for the white-collar profile; @tbl-ch8-support
asks a coarser question, how far each variable extends within each
recorded type.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ch8-support
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Predictor ranges within each recorded occupation type."
ch8_ranges <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(d, d$type), function(g) {
  data.frame(n = nrow(g),
    Education = sprintf("%.2f--%.2f",
                        min(g$education), max(g$education)),
    Prestige = sprintf("%.1f--%.1f",
                       min(g$prestige), max(g$prestige)),
    Women = sprintf("%.2f--%.2f", min(g$women), max(g$women)))
}))
knitr::kable(cbind(Type = rownames(ch8_ranges), ch8_ranges),
  row.names = FALSE)
```

Blue-collar education ends at 10.93 years, below the professional minimum
of 11.09, so comparing those types at the same education crosses a gap
with no records. The model still returns predictions there, but software
output does not create observations: a lack of support limits what the
data can say about a comparison without making the comparison undefined.

A display of fitted values can respect support. @fig-ch8-grid holds
prestige at 30, 50, or 70 in *m1* and draws education only over the
values observed within 7.5 prestige points of each; the width is a
stated display choice, not a formal guarantee. The lines are parallel
and fall gently because the additive *m1* has one education slope,
$-0.2179$ (Section 3.1), at every prestige, and the higher-prestige lines
sit over higher education. Because the display conditions on prestige
alone, it illustrates the plotting choice rather than support for the
full-model profile.

```{r}
#| label: ch8-grid
#| echo: false
#| results: hide
ch8_grid <- data.frame()
for (p0 in c(30, 50, 70)) {
  nearby <- d[abs(d$prestige - p0) <= 7.5, ]
  one_grid <- data.frame(
    education = seq(min(nearby$education), max(nearby$education),
                    length.out = 40),
    prestige = p0, Profile = paste("Prestige", p0)
  )
  ch8_grid <- rbind(ch8_grid, one_grid)
}
ch8_grid$fit <- predict(m1, newdata = ch8_grid)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ch8-grid
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Neighborhood-restricted fitted profiles from the education-and-prestige model."
#| fig-alt: >
#|   Three gently decreasing parallel lines represent fitted income
#|   across education at prestige 30, 50, and 70. Their education
#|   ranges differ, reflecting the declared neighborhoods.
#| fig-width: 6.1
#| fig-height: 3.5
ggplot2::ggplot(ch8_grid,
  ggplot2::aes(education, fit, linetype = Profile)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = .8) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Education (years)",
    y = "Fitted income (thousand 1971 dollars)") +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

**Collinearity** means that a predictor is strongly linearly related to
the other predictors, so they largely predict it, and it costs
precision. The auxiliary $R^2$ from regressing education on the other
predictors, .8765, measures how strongly: they account for most of
education's variation, and education's **variance inflation factor** is

$$
VIF_E=\frac{1}{1-R^2_{E\mid P,W,T}}\approx8.0968,
\qquad \sqrt{VIF_E}\approx2.8455.
$$

@fig-ch8-vif draws the SE multiplier $\sqrt{VIF}$ against the auxiliary
$R^2$ for the three continuous predictors. The curve rises slowly at
first, so women (auxiliary $R^2$ .2312, multiplier 1.1405) loses little
precision, and it climbs steeply beyond about .8, where prestige (.8066,
multiplier 2.2738) and education sit.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ch8-vif
#| fig-cap: "The SE multiplier grows steeply as the other predictors account for more of a predictor's variation."
#| fig-alt: "A curve of the square root of the VIF against the auxiliary R-squared rises slowly from 1 at zero and steeply beyond about 0.8. Points mark women near 0.23 with multiplier 1.14, prestige near 0.81 with 2.27, and education near 0.88 with 2.85."
#| fig-width: 6.1
#| fig-height: 3.1
ch8_vif <- car::vif(m2)[c("women", "prestige", "education"), 1]
ch8_vif_points <- data.frame(name = c("Women", "Prestige", "Education"),
                             r2 = 1 - 1 / ch8_vif,
                             multiplier = sqrt(ch8_vif))
ch8_vif_curve <- data.frame(r2 = seq(0, .95, length.out = 200))
ch8_vif_curve$multiplier <- sqrt(1 / (1 - ch8_vif_curve$r2))
ggplot2::ggplot(ch8_vif_curve, ggplot2::aes(r2, multiplier)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = .8) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(data = ch8_vif_points, size = 2.3,
                      colour = "#245C78") +
  ggplot2::geom_text(data = ch8_vif_points,
                     ggplot2::aes(label = name),
                     hjust = 1.15, vjust = -.4, size = 3.2) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Auxiliary R-squared of the predictor on the others",
                y = "SE multiplier, square root of VIF")
```

Under the classical model, holding the residual variance and education's
total variation fixed, education's SE is 2.8455 times what it would be in
an orthogonal design, where education is uncorrelated with the other
predictors. This compares two variance formulas: deleting a predictor
would change the comparison and can change the residual variance, so a
VIF is not a deletion rule, and near collinearity does not by itself
bias the coefficient under the maintained zero-conditional-mean model.

### Sensitivity to curvature and to one record

A component-plus-residual plot adds the fitted prestige term back to
each residual, $e_i+\widehat\beta_P P_i$. In @fig-ch8-partial-residual
the smooth bends upward at high prestige, away from the straight fitted
component. That motivates a declared form sensitivity; it does not show
that any one curve is the true process.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ch8-partial-residual
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The prestige component plus residual in the full additive model."
#| fig-alt: >
#|   A component-plus-residual scatterplot has a positive trend.
#|   A curved smooth bends upward at high prestige relative to the
#|   straight fitted component.
#| fig-width: 6.1
#| fig-height: 3.5
ch8_partial <- data.frame(
  prestige = d$prestige,
  component = residuals(m2) + coef(m2)["prestige"] * d$prestige
)
ggplot2::ggplot(ch8_partial, ggplot2::aes(prestige, component)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(shape = 1) +
  ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE,
                      colour = "black", linetype = 2) +
  ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE,
                      colour = "black") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Prestige", y = "Component plus residual")
```

The refit adds a squared prestige term to *m2*. The two fits are
**nested**: they share the outcome and the 98 rows, and the smaller
fit's predictors are a subset of the larger fit's. Chapter 6's
nested-model $F$ compared an additive and a full model of the
feedback-and-practice study, and the same comparison applies here with
continuous predictors. Its null hypothesis is that the squared-prestige
coefficient is zero, so that *m2*'s mean function suffices; the
statistic sets the residual sum of squares that the added term removes
against the larger fit's residual variance, on 1 and $98-7=91$ degrees
of freedom. A small $p$-value says the term removes more variation than
the error scale would ordinarily produce under that null. It does not
make the enlarged equation the correct mean function, and it is not a
rule for choosing a model; Chapter 9 develops the general comparison.

\Needspace{26\baselineskip}

```{r}
#| label: ch8-form-sensitivity
#| echo: true
ch8_curve <- update(m2, . ~ . + I(prestige^2))
anova(m2, ch8_curve)
c(full_education = unname(coef(m2)["education"]),
  curve_education = unname(coef(ch8_curve)["education"]))
```

The comparison gives $F(1,91)=6.736$ and $p=.011$, and education moves
from 0.1164 to $-0.0298$; in the enlarged equation the prestige slope,
$\beta_P+2\beta_{P^2}P$, depends on prestige. This is a focused
sensitivity for Pair 2, not a replacement for the prediction rule that
Pair 3 fixed in advance.

General managers have the largest Cook's distance, about 0.4467; a high
income relative to the model is not proof of an error. Refitting the
formula to the other 97 records, as the Computer Lab does, moves
education from 0.1164 to 0.4372. We keep the full-data estimate and
disclose the sensitivity: excluding a record needs evidence about its
coding, measurement, or distinctiveness, never a more attractive
$p$-value. @tbl-ch8-checks collects what each check shows and what
follows for the answer.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{30\baselineskip}
```

| Check | What is visible here | Consequence for the answer |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Functional form | Adding a prestige-squared term changes the education slope to about $-0.0298$ | Treat the additive form as a working approximation; do not silently reinterpret it as an exact conditional law |
| Spread | HC3 raises the education SE from 0.2752 to 0.3823 | Show sensitivity; a robust SE does not repair all model problems |
| Influence | Removing the record for general managers, which has the largest Cook's distance, gives an education slope about 0.4372 | Inspect the record and disclose sensitivity; do not delete it merely to obtain a preferred result |
| Collinearity | Education's auxiliary $R^2$ is .8765 | Little education variation remains after the other predictors; separate conditional coefficients can be imprecise |
| Joint support | Professional and blue-collar education ranges do not overlap | Cross-type comparisons at common covariates may depend heavily on extrapolation |
| Dependence and scope | Occupational aggregates have shared economic and classification contexts | Independence and same-source transport are assumptions, not verified by a residual plot |

: Checks change the bounded answer rather than producing one omnibus pass/fail score. {#tbl-ch8-checks tbl-colwidths="[19,38,43]"}

Appendix B gives the formulas for Cook's distance, the HC3 covariance,
the generalized VIF, and the model-comparison criteria; the results
needed to interpret the answer are all in this section.

## Fitted and Standardized Quantities {#sec-ch8-quantities}

The fitted model also gives quantities for particular profiles: a fitted
mean with its two intervals, and an average over a named set of
profiles. These are teaching extensions of the model, not further
answers the study owes; Pair 2 remains about $\beta_E$.

### A fitted mean and its two intervals

For a complete input row, `predict()` returns two intervals:
`interval = "confidence"` concerns the model's mean at that profile, and
`interval = "prediction"` concerns one new outcome at the same profile.
Both use the full fitted model and its classical assumptions.

\Needspace{17\baselineskip}

```{r}
#| label: ch8-profile-predict-check
#| echo: true
profile <- data.frame(education = 11, prestige = 45, women = 50,
                      type = factor("wc", levels = levels(d$type)))
predict(m2, newdata = profile, interval = "confidence")
predict(m2, newdata = profile, interval = "prediction")
```

Where do these intervals come from? Collect the coefficient multipliers
of the Section 2.3 profile in $\mathbf x_*=(1,11,45,50,0,1)^{\mathsf T}$,
in the order intercept, education, prestige, women, professional
indicator, and white-collar indicator; the superscript $\mathsf T$
denotes the transpose. With $\widehat{\mathbf V}$, the coefficient
covariance of Section 3.2, the fitted mean and its estimated classical
variance are

$$
\widehat m_*=\mathbf x_*^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat m_*)=\mathbf x_*^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\mathbf V}\mathbf x_*,
\quad \widehat{\mathbf V}=\operatorname{vcov}(m2).
$$

The variance includes the coefficient variances **and their
covariances**: two terms $a\widehat\beta_j+b\widehat\beta_k$ contribute
$a^2\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat\beta_j)+
b^2\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat\beta_k)+
2ab\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}(\widehat\beta_j,\widehat\beta_k)$.
Adding coefficient SEs, or ignoring the covariances, is a different
calculation, and the square root comes only after the variance is
complete. Here the fitted mean is 5.5886, its variance 0.308, and its SE
0.5549 thousand dollars, giving the fitted-mean interval
$[4.4865,6.6908]$ that `predict()` printed.

**One new outcome** adds its own error variance, $s^2=6.8575$, so its SE
is $\sqrt{s^2+\mathbf x_*^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\mathbf V}\mathbf x_*}\approx2.6768$
and its interval $[0.2722,10.9051]$. @fig-ch8-bands draws both intervals
across the white-collar education range at prestige 45 and women 50. The
dark fitted-mean band is narrowest near education 11.2, about 2.2
thousand dollars wide, and widens toward the edges of the records, to
about 3.1 at 9.17 years. The light band for one new occupation stays
between about 10.6 and 10.9 wide along the whole range, because the new
occupation's error variance, 6.8575, dominates a fitted-mean variance of
about 0.3.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ch8-bands
#| fig-cap: "Two 95% intervals for a white-collar profile at prestige 45 and women 50, across the white-collar education range."
#| fig-alt: "A nearly flat fitted line runs from about 5.4 to 5.8 thousand dollars as education rises from 9.17 to 12.79 years. A narrow dark band around it, the fitted-mean interval, is narrowest near 11 years and widens toward both ends. A much wider light band, the interval for one new occupation, runs from about 0 to 11 thousand dollars along the whole range. A dotted vertical line marks education 11."
#| fig-width: 6.1
#| fig-height: 3.3
wc_range <- range(d$education[d$type == "wc"])
band <- data.frame(education = seq(wc_range[1], wc_range[2],
                                   length.out = 60),
                   prestige = 45, women = 50,
                   type = factor("wc", levels = levels(d$type)))
mean_band <- predict(m2, newdata = band, interval = "confidence")
new_band <- predict(m2, newdata = band, interval = "prediction")
band <- cbind(band, fit = mean_band[, "fit"],
              mean_lwr = mean_band[, "lwr"], mean_upr = mean_band[, "upr"],
              new_lwr = new_band[, "lwr"], new_upr = new_band[, "upr"])
ggplot2::ggplot(band, ggplot2::aes(education)) +
  ggplot2::geom_ribbon(ggplot2::aes(ymin = new_lwr, ymax = new_upr),
                       fill = "grey88") +
  ggplot2::geom_ribbon(ggplot2::aes(ymin = mean_lwr, ymax = mean_upr),
                       fill = "#9DB9CC") +
  ggplot2::geom_line(ggplot2::aes(y = fit), linewidth = .8) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 11, linetype = 3) +
  ggplot2::annotate("text", x = 12.7, y = c(10.2, 6.75), hjust = 1,
                    size = 3.1,
                    label = c("One new occupation", "Fitted mean")) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Education (years), over the white-collar range",
                y = "Income (thousand 1971 dollars)")
```

Both intervals rest on the independent, Normal, common-variance model,
which the checks of Section 4 qualify rather than confirm; replacing
$\widehat{\mathbf V}$ with HC3 alone does not estimate a new outcome's
conditional error distribution. Neither interval says how accurately a
learning rule predicts held-out records; that is Pair 3's question.

### Standardizing over the observed profiles

A standardized fitted value averages over a named set of profiles rather
than using one. Copy the 98 observed profiles, change every type to
white-collar, predict each fitted value, and average them with equal
weights.

\Needspace{11\baselineskip}

```{r}
#| label: ch8-standardization-first
#| echo: true
white_profiles <- d
white_profiles$type <- factor("wc", levels = levels(d$type))
mean(predict(m2, newdata = white_profiles))
```

The result, 7.0164, is an average of model predictions after a specified
change of profile, not the observed white-collar group mean. For type
$g$ and fixed nonnegative weights $w_i$ summing to one,

$$
\widehat\mu_g^{\mathrm{std}}=\sum_i w_i\mathbf x_{ig}^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=\mathbf a_g^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},\qquad \mathbf a_g=\sum_i w_i\mathbf x_{ig},
$$

where the design vector $\mathbf x_{ig}$ holds the six coefficient
multipliers of observed profile $i$, as $\mathbf x_*$ does in Section
5.1, after its type is set to $g$; $\mathbf a_g$ is their weighted
average. With empirical weights $w_i=1/98$ this
standardizes over these 98 profiles, not over a national population, and
treating the profiles and weights as fixed gives the estimated variance
$\mathbf a_g^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\mathbf V}\mathbf a_g$. For
white-collar, $\mathbf a_{\mathrm{wc}}^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}$
returns 7.0164 with SE 0.6177 and classical interval $[5.7896,8.2432]$.
The variance keeps the covariances among the 98 predictions, which share
the fitted coefficients, so averaging their interval endpoints would be
a different calculation. The Computer Lab computes
$\mathbf a_{\mathrm{wc}}$ and repeats the operation for each type;
@tbl-ch8-standardized sets the results beside each type's observed mean
income.

\Needspace{9\baselineskip}

| Type | Observed mean | Standardized estimate | SE | Lower | Upper |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| bc | 5.3741 | 6.7811 | 0.6942 | 5.4023 | 8.1598 |
| prof | 10.5595 | 7.1053 | 0.9011 | 5.3156 | 8.8950 |
| wc | 5.0523 | 7.0164 | 0.6177 | 5.7896 | 8.2432 |

: Observed type means and empirical-profile standardization under the full additive model. {#tbl-ch8-standardized tbl-colwidths="[12,18,22,14,17,17]"}

The observed means differ sharply: professional occupations average
10.5595 thousand dollars, about twice the other two types, but they also
have more education, higher prestige, and different percentages of
women. The standardized estimates give every type the same 98 profiles,
so they differ only by the type coefficients, 0.3242 for professional
and 0.2353 for white-collar relative to blue-collar.

Because *m2* is linear and additive in the continuous predictors, its
average fitted value equals its fitted value at their means (education
averages 10.7951 years); with squared terms, interactions, or a
nonlinear response function, the prediction at the means need not equal
the mean prediction. Any other fixed weighting used for all three
types, whether another named set of profiles or unequal weights on these
98, would move the three standardized levels but leave their differences
at the type coefficients.

Relabelling every profile professional or white-collar creates some
combinations the records do not support, and averaging does not remove
that problem; the white-collar profile of Section 5.1 is a different,
locally supported quantity. Standardization alone neither identifies a
causal effect nor validates out-of-sample performance.

\Needspace{12\baselineskip}

## The Held-Out Prediction Question {#sec-ch8-prediction}

### Learning rules and the loss

A learning rule says how training records become a prediction equation.
Our two rules are fixed: education-only OLS, and the full additive OLS
equation with education, prestige, women, and type. OLS **fits** by
minimizing squared training errors; we separately choose the **mean
absolute error (MAE)** to evaluate the predictions in income units.

A prediction opportunity here is a hypothetical same-source occupation
whose predictors are all available before its income is used, not a
forecast from information that arrives later. The records cannot show
that this exchangeability holds for other countries, periods, individual
workers, or types absent from the dictionary.

For held-out outcomes $y_i$ and predictions $\widehat y_i^{(-)}$ fitted
without those outcomes,

$$
MAE=\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}}
       \sum_{i\in\mathrm{test}}\left|y_i-\widehat y_i^{(-)}\right|.
$$

A smaller MAE means a smaller average absolute error on the evaluated
cases, not a better prediction for every case.

### Shared ten-fold validation

In shared ten-fold cross-validation the 98 records are divided into ten
folds, and each fold takes a turn as the held-out set: both rules are
fitted to the other records and predict the held-out cases
(@fig-ch8-folds), and the 98 case-level errors are then pooled.
@tbl-ch8-validation records the protocol.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ch8-folds
#| fig-cap: "Shared held-out cases let two fixed learning rules face the same prediction task."
#| fig-alt: "A training-record box branches to education-only OLS and full OLS. Both arrows lead to predictions for the same held-out records, then to paired absolute errors. The diagram is repeated over ten folds."
#| fig-width: 6.3
#| fig-height: 3.3
par(mar = c(.2, .2, .2, .2))
plot.new()
plot.window(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 5))
boxtext <- function(x1, y1, x2, y2, label, fill = "#EFF4F7") {
  rect(x1, y1, x2, y2, col = fill, border = "#426278")
  text((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2, label, cex = .9)
}
boxtext(.1, 1.8, 2.3, 3.2, "Training records\n88 or 89")
boxtext(3.1, 3.1, 6.2, 4.4, "Education-only OLS")
boxtext(3.1, .6, 6.2, 1.9, "Full additive OLS")
boxtext(7, 1.8, 9.9, 3.2, "Same held-out cases\nPaired absolute errors")
arrows(2.3, 2.8, 3.1, 3.6, length = .08)
arrows(2.3, 2.2, 3.1, 1.4, length = .08)
arrows(6.2, 3.6, 7, 2.8, length = .08)
arrows(6.2, 1.4, 7, 2.2, length = .08)
text(5, .12, "Repeat across ten folds; pool the 98 case-level errors.", cex = .9)
```

\Needspace{24\baselineskip}

| Decision | Frozen teaching protocol | Why it matters |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Candidates | Education-only and the declared full additive OLS rule | No search for the best-looking model after validation |
| Folds | Shared balanced random ten-fold assignment, seed 80806 | Both rules face the same held-out cases |
| Training sizes | Eight fits use 88 records; two use 89 | Risk concerns those training sizes, not a model trained on all 98 |
| Preparation | Same 98 complete records; fixed income/1,000 conversion and type dictionary | No outcome-informed preprocessing; selection still limits scope |
| Estimability | Every training set must contain all three types and have full column rank | Stop rather than silently substitute a different rule |
| Summary | Pool absolute errors over all 98 held-out cases | Each case receives equal weight; folds of different size do not |
| Sensitivity | 200 new resplits of the same records, seed 80807 | Describes sensitivity to splitting, not new independent studies |

: The internal-validation protocol was fixed before this teaching comparison. {#tbl-ch8-validation tbl-colwidths="[20,42,38]"}

This is a retrospective reanalysis of familiar data, so "fixed before
this comparison" is not a claim of historical preregistration. It means
that the candidates were not revised after the primary errors were seen.
The sensitivity refits of Section 4 are not added to the candidate set.
The code below runs one fold of this protocol: the fold that holds the
first source record.

\Needspace{27\baselineskip}

```{r}
#| label: ch8-one-fold
#| echo: true
RNGkind("Mersenne-Twister", "Inversion", "Rejection")
set.seed(80806)
fold <- sample(rep(seq_len(10), length.out = nrow(d)))
held_fold <- fold[1]
train <- d[fold != held_fold, ]
held <- d[fold == held_fold, ]
c(fold = held_fold, training = nrow(train), held_out = nrow(held))
fold_simple <- lm(income_k ~ education, data = train)
fold_full <- lm(income_k ~ education + prestige + women + type,
                data = train)
first_case <- d[1, ]
first_predictions <- c(
  Education = unname(predict(fold_simple, first_case)),
  Full = unname(predict(fold_full, first_case)))
first_predictions
abs(first_predictions - first_case$income_k)
```

Government administrators, the first source record, fall in fold 9,
leaving 89 training and 9 held-out records; both fits exclude the record,
and the code predicts it. The full rule is estimable only if every
training set contains all three types, which the Computer Lab checks for
every fold together with the fitted ranks. The Lab also provides the
complete ten-fold function and the 200 resplits, and Chapter 13 develops
held-out validation fully.

No held-out outcome is used to estimate a coefficient. Learned
preprocessing, such as scaling, imputation, or variable selection, would
also have to be fitted on training records only; a fixed unit conversion
such as dollars to thousands is not learned.

### Held-out errors and resplits

For government administrators, observed income is 12.351 thousand
dollars. The full-rule prediction is 11.5948, giving

$$
|12.351-11.5948|=0.7562,
$$

and the education-only prediction is 8.9461, giving
$|12.351-8.9461|=3.4049$.
This record favors the full rule, but one record is not the comparison;
@tbl-ch8-mae pools all 98 errors.

| Learning rule | Held-out MAE (thousand dollars) |
|:--|--:|
| Education-only OLS | 2.4031 |
| Full additive OLS | 1.5412 |
| Difference: full minus education-only | $-0.8619$ |

: Case-weighted absolute errors from the frozen shared-fold comparison. {#tbl-ch8-mae tbl-colwidths="[60,40]"}

The full rule's average held-out absolute error is about 862 dollars
lower. Because the two errors are subtracted for **each same case**
before averaging, differences in difficulty between cases cannot favor
either rule through different test sets. The same predictions give the
root mean squared error, which weights large errors more heavily: 3.5051
for education-only and 2.7111 for the full rule, the same preference
here, although the two losses need not agree in other data.

What exactly is estimated? Eight test folds contain 10 cases predicted
from 88 training records, and two contain 9 cases predicted from 89, so
the pooled quantity targets the mixture

$$
R_{\mathrm{mix}}=\frac{80}{98}R_{88}+\frac{18}{98}R_{89},
$$

where $R_m$ is the expected absolute error of the specified learning rule
trained on $m$ eligible same-source records and used on a new one. Pair 3
compares the two rules' $R_{\mathrm{mix}}$; it does not directly estimate
the performance of the single equation fitted to all 98 records.

The 200 resplits give full-minus-education MAE differences from $-0.914$
to $-0.741$, all favoring the full rule. That range shows stability
across the examined splits, but it is **not a 95% interval**: the same
cases are reused, training sets overlap, and the splits are not
independent studies, which is also why we do not test the ten fold
errors as if they were independent. Uncertainty across newly drawn
training samples is not quantified, so the advantage is provisional.

The comparison supports lower internal held-out error for the full rule
in these records under this protocol. It does not isolate the predictive
contribution of education, because the rules differ by prestige, women,
and type together, and it does not establish external transport,
individual earnings prediction, or a causal education effect.

\Needspace{14\baselineskip}

## Reading and Evaluating the Three Answers {#sec-ch8-coordinate}

### The study report

The report below gathers the analyses of Sections 1--6. It is our
teaching record, not a statement by the source investigators.

> **R0 -- Common record and declared scope.** We analyzed the 98 complete
> occupation records described in @sec-ch8-questions. Income was
> scaled to thousand
> 1971 Canadian dollars. Education and income were historical occupational
> averages; prestige came from an earlier rating survey. We retained the
> same rows for all three questions and make no claim of verified probability
> sampling or randomized education.
>
> **R1 -- Marginal answer.** Across these records the education-only
> least-squares slope was 0.883 thousand dollars per year. This is a
> descriptive linear summary: occupations with more education tended to
> have higher average income. It is not an individual or causal effect.
>
> **R2 -- Conditional answer.** The intended estimand was the linear
> conditional-mean education coefficient $\beta_E$, comparing education at the
> same prestige, percentage of women, and occupational type. Its fitted
> estimate was $b_E=0.1164$, with a classical 95% interval [$-0.4302$, 0.6631]
> under the independent linear conditional-mean working model with common
> variance. HC3 gave [$-0.6429$, 0.8758]. Influence, functional-form, and support
> checks limit that model's interpretation. The direction and practically
> relevant magnitude remain unresolved under these calculations; the result
> does not establish no conditional relationship.
>
> **R3 -- Prediction answer.** The two fixed OLS learning rules were compared
> with the shared ten-fold protocol in @sec-ch8-prediction. The full
> rule had MAE
> 1.5412 versus 2.4031 for education-only, difference $-0.8619$. The examined
> resplits all favored the full rule. This is internal evidence about
> learning procedures trained on 88/89 eligible records under the stated
> same-source exchangeability assumptions. Lower expected error is a
> provisional conclusion because new-sample uncertainty is not quantified;
> this is not external validation of a final 98-record equation.
>
> **R4 -- Synthesis.** Education has a positive marginal linear association
> with income in these historical records. Its conditional association is
> imprecisely resolved by the specified additive model, while the full
> learning rule predicts the held-out records more accurately than the
> education-only rule. These conclusions answer different questions and
> do not establish that changing education would change income.

### Functions and traces in the report

Reading starts by locating what each passage does. In Chapter 1's
terms, a component is a logical function, such as STAT-E or SUB-J, and
the report's study-specific content serves it. One passage can serve
several functions. R0, for example, identifies the records for STAT-E
and supplies their historical context for SUB-E. It would become
justification (J) content only if it offered a reason connecting those
records to an inference; "we used R" offers none. @tbl-ch8-traces lists
each function once, with the content shared by the three pairs and the
content specific to each.

| Function | Shared or pair-specific content | Trace in this teaching record |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **STAT-E** | Named 98 rows, variables, exclusions, and computations' inputs | R0; the row audit and import code in @sec-ch8-questions |
| **SUB-E** | Occupations rather than workers; historical dollars, education, ratings, and types | R0; variable/source descriptions |
| **STAT-J** | Pair 1: fixed-record least-squares definition. Pair 2: declared stochastic model and uncertainty conditions. Pair 3: held-out fitting, fixed rules, loss, and exchangeability | R1--R3; model declaration; validation protocol and code |
| **SUB-J** | Reasons connecting those measurements and comparisons to historical occupational income, with limits on individual, current, and causal interpretations | R0--R3; unit/time explanations and prediction-opportunity definition |
| **STAT-I** | Pair 1's 0.8830 slope; Pair 2's 0.1164 estimate, intervals, coefficient test and checks; Pair 3's case-level errors, MAEs, and split sensitivity | @sec-ch8-estimate through @sec-ch8-prediction; R1--R3 |
| **STAT-C** | Descriptive positive marginal slope; unresolved conditional slope under the model; smaller internal error for the full rule under the protocol | R1, R2, and R3 respectively |
| **SUB-I** | Interpret years, income units, conditioning, and prediction errors in the named historical occupation setting | Worked substitutions and error calculation; R1--R3 |
| **SUB-C** | Each question-facing answer with its own limits; none supplies a causal or individual-earnings answer | R1--R3; their distinctions preserved in R4 |

: Reading the linked-layer functions without three duplicate maps. {#tbl-ch8-traces tbl-colwidths="[15,47,38]"}

SUB-E situates the evidence, SUB-J **augments and contextualizes** the
statistical justification, SUB-I interprets the inference, and SUB-C
bounds the substantive answer. Sharing a dataset does not make Pair 2's
independent-error model into Pair 3's validation procedure.

For each supporting statement, record what the report says and where
the reader finds it: in the report, the data documentation, or the
executable calculations. Gaps and conflicts are stated in ordinary
prose. R2 states the independence assumption, for example, but nothing in
the record shows that independence holds under the original selection of
occupations; a stated assumption and evidence for it are different
information. The unit conversion, by contrast, makes reading 0.883
thousand dollars as about 883 dollars traceable. This record contains no
conflicting source, though a real study may contain incompatible
descriptions to record and investigate. A reason's documentary status is
simply what has been stated or located and which support is missing; it
is not a quality score or a set of categories to learn.

Professional knowledge helps identify a trace's function but does not
license adding an unreported design feature. An invalid reason such as
"all rows are in the same dataset, therefore they are independent" is
still **stated J**, whose adequacy is judged separately: reading records
the reason actually offered, not a repaired one.

### Evaluating each answer

Evaluation now judges the quality of the reasoning just identified.
Chapter 1's six questions apply to each argument (@tbl-ch8-quality); they
are not six scores to total.

| Quality-evaluation question | Application to these arguments |
|:--|:--|
| **Question alignment** | R1 matches its finite-record slope. R2 names $\beta_E$, its fitted estimate, the conditioning set, and the model extension. R3 names the learning procedure, loss, and training sizes rather than substituting a coefficient test. |
| **Evidence integrity** | The 102-to-98 accounting and common rows are explicit. Missing type still limits what is represented. CV excludes held-out outcomes from fitting; source selection is not repaired by that procedure. |
| **Justification adequacy** | Least squares is sufficient for the declared finite description. Pair 2's model conditions and Pair 3's same-source exchangeability remain assumptions with incomplete empirical support. Statistical computation alone cannot establish them. |
| **Inferential adequacy** | The slope, intervals, error arithmetic, and comparisons are reproducible. Neither zero-crossing nor a large p-value proves absence; repeated folds are not independent replication. Substantive reasoning must retain those distinctions. |
| **Transition fidelity** | Occupation-level average income remains occupation-level average income; partial adjustment is not a causal intervention, and model fit is not held-out performance. |
| **Claim calibration** | R1 remains finite and historical; R2 reports unresolved magnitude/direction rather than no relationship; R3 remains internal and procedure-specific. No claim extends to individual workers or modern populations. |

: Apply the six questions before evaluating the study-level synthesis. {#tbl-ch8-quality tbl-colwidths="[28,72]"}

Each question receives a judgment with a reason: **adequate for this
purpose**, **needs revision**, **insufficient information to judge**, or
**not applicable**. The record is adequate, for example, to check Pair
3's held-out computations, but it gives insufficient information to
establish exchangeability with an external population.

\Needspace{6\baselineskip}

Each whole pair then receives its own conclusion:

- **Pair 1: supported as stated**, as an accurate bounded description of
  the retained records.
- **Pair 2: supported as stated**, as the explicitly conditional,
  unresolved working-model answer about $\beta_E$ actually reported. This
  certifies neither the model nor a population relationship, and a claim
  that the true national conditional slope is zero would not be
  supported.
- **Pair 3: supported as stated**, as a qualified internal comparison with
  its assumptions and limits. External superiority of the final
  all-record fitted equation is **not assessable from the accessible
  record**, and it is not the answer being accepted.

The other whole-pair conclusions are **supported only after narrowing or
revision**, **not supported**, and **not assessable from the accessible
record**. A correctly reported inconclusive answer can be supported as
stated; it is not rejected for failing to answer a stronger question.

### Is the synthesis coherent?

Coordinated questions add one evaluation question, **Cross-question
coherence**: does the synthesis preserve the distinct questions,
estimands, methods, analytic statuses, uncertainty, and limits of the
separate answers? We introduce it here; Supplementary B develops it
further but is not needed to apply it.

R4 is coherent because it reports three distinct outcomes: a positive
marginal slope, an unresolved conditional slope, and better internal
prediction can hold together without contradiction. Now consider this
alternative:

> Once the other predictors were controlled, education had no effect;
> nevertheless, the significant full regression proves it will predict
> workers' incomes accurately.

Reading first identifies the inference and claim it offers. Evaluation
then finds three failures: "no effect" substitutes a causal null for the
conditional-association answer, an omnibus significance test is not
held-out validation, and occupations have become workers. The corrected
synthesis is R4, not a fourth overarching argument that erases the
separate conclusions.

### Carrying out a study with several questions

Sections 7.1 to 7.4 read and evaluate a finished report. The approach
also has an auxiliary use: Chapter 1's construction workflow, which
serves researchers carrying out a study and is not a required reading
sequence. Each question keeps its own six-stage
cycle from Chapter 1, and for coordinated questions Supplementary B's
extension aligns the plans at Stage 3 and adds Stage 7 for synthesis.

In **Understand and plan**, researchers review the problem and
literature, frame questions and candidate answers, and align design,
measurement, estimands, evidence acquisition, and inference. "Separate
questions" means separately owed conclusions; estimands that one
integrated conclusion needs would be planned as strands instead. The
extended **Stage 3, Plan and align prospectively across questions**,
fixes common rows and units but distinct marginal, model-based, and
validation plans.

In **Produce and complete**, **Stage 4, Produce or
acquire and document evidence**, designates each question's records;
**Stage 5, Estimate, check, and analyse**, performs the computations; and
**Stage 6, Contextualize, interpret, and complete the bounded answer**,
finishes each answer with its actual limits. **Stage 7, Give explicit
outcomes and synthesize**, records all outcomes and brings them together
without creating an omnibus argument.

Iteration stays within a phase: a same-anchor error correction or a
justified uncertainty repair can reopen Phase 2 work, but a newly
preferred outcome, question mode, or estimand requires a new or revised
cycle, reusing records where appropriate and disclosing its timing. A
newly chosen causal question cannot be "narrowed" into association and
treated as answered, and this reanalysis does not claim that the
historical data were collected for our three questions.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{22\baselineskip}
```

## Reading Bridge {#sec-ch8-summary}

Multiple regression adds conditional comparisons, not automatic causal
control. Subtracting fitted means showed what a coefficient compares;
residualizing connected it to covariance; residual, influence, support,
and precision checks each bounded the answer differently; a fitted
profile and a standardized average extended the conditional model; and
held-out errors answered a separately owed question. The occupation study
owed three answers, a finite-record marginal description, a working-model
conditional interval with unresolved magnitude, and a qualified internal
prediction comparison, and its shared records made the questions
coordinated without making their justifications identical. The next
regression question is different: might the education comparison itself
vary with another predictor? Chapter 9 first collects the tools this
chapter used only briefly (factors with several levels and their
contrasts, nested model comparison and information criteria, changed
predictor and outcome forms, and robust, clustered, and bootstrap
uncertainty) and transfers the reading to Project STAR, where a
randomized design supplies a different warrant. Chapter 10 then extends
the interaction reasoning of Chapters 4 and 6 to regression.

\Needspace{22\baselineskip}

### Key terms {.unnumbered}

Use this short reference to revisit the concepts introduced here. The
Part One Concept Reference gives the broader reference and the principal home
of each concept; the simple-regression, interval, ANOVA, and reading
vocabulary used in this chapter is explained in Chapters 1--4 and 7.

| Term and common alternatives | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| Multiple regression (additive model) | A fitted equation in which the outcome's mean is the sum of an intercept and one term per predictor. Each coefficient compares fitted means at the same values of the other predictors; the additive form assumes each comparison is the same across those values. |
| Partial slope (conditional coefficient; adjusted coefficient) | The difference in fitted outcome per one-unit difference in one predictor, holding the model's other predictors fixed. Its meaning depends on the conditioning set named with it; it is not an intervention effect or a claim about unmeasured differences. |
| Indicator variable (dummy variable) and reference category | A 0/1 variable marking membership in one category of a factor; a factor with $J$ levels needs $J-1$ indicators, and the omitted level is the reference. The intercept refers to the reference category; each indicator coefficient is a difference from it at the same other predictors. Releveling changes coordinates, not fitted values. |
| Partial regression (residualization; added-variable form) | Regressing both the outcome and one predictor on the other predictors, then relating their residuals. The residual slope equals the partial slope; the residual correlation is the partial correlation, unit-free. |
| Coefficient covariance matrix | The estimated variances and covariances of the fitted coefficients (`vcov()` in R). Any linear combination of coefficients, such as a fitted mean or a contrast, has variance $\mathbf c^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\mathbf V}\mathbf c$; adding SEs or ignoring covariances is a different, incorrect calculation. |
| Variance inflation factor (VIF) | One divided by one minus the $R^2$ from regressing a predictor on the other predictors. Its square root multiplies that coefficient's SE relative to an orthogonal design, holding residual variance fixed; it describes precision, not bias, and is not a deletion rule. |
| Joint support (covariate hull) | Whether a combination of predictor values lies within the region where observations actually occur, not merely within each variable's separate range. A fitted value outside joint support is extrapolation even if each coordinate is observed somewhere. |
| Standardization over a named distribution (model-averaged fitted value) | Averaging the model's fitted values after setting one predictor to a chosen value for every profile in a declared set with fixed weights. Its uncertainty uses the coefficient covariance; it is not an observed group mean, a causal effect, or held-out performance. |
| Learning rule (learning procedure) | A fixed recipe that turns training records into a prediction equation, such as fitting a declared OLS formula. Prediction performance concerns the rule at stated training sizes, not one final fitted equation. |
| Cross-validation (held-out validation) | Dividing records into folds, fitting a rule on the other folds, predicting the held-out fold, and pooling the errors so that no outcome contributes to its own prediction. Resplits describe sensitivity to the partition, not new independent studies. |
| Mean absolute error (MAE) | The average absolute difference between held-out outcomes and their predictions, in outcome units. It is an evaluation loss chosen separately from the squared-error criterion that OLS minimizes. |
| Cross-question coherence | The additional evaluation question for coordinated answers: does the synthesis preserve the distinct questions, estimands, methods, uncertainty, and limits of the separate answers rather than merging them into one omnibus claim? |

: Selected concepts for multiple regression across coordinated questions. {#tbl-ch08-key-terms tbl-colwidths="[28,72]"}
